title: Lazarus, Come Out!
lead: Not even the grave is the limit of what God can do.
questions: Which matter in my life has “already been four days” in the tomb, and am I ready to let Jesus come up to that grave?
Do I let myself and others weep at gravesides, or do I demand a faith that forbids tears?
Who around me has already come out of the grave but still walks wrapped in the grave clothes of the past, and what can I help them unwrap?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The third fear of our section: the tomb is sealed. From Bethany, a village whose name most likely means “house of the poor,” a message reaches Jesus that is a model of prayer: “Lord, the one You love is sick.” No instructions, no “come at once”; the sisters tell Him what is happening and leave the rest to His love. And Jesus stays two more days. The arithmetic hidden in the text lifts an old charge from Him: since after a day’s journey He found that Lazarus “had already spent four days in the tomb,” His friend had died before the messenger even arrived. The delay killed no one. But those who were waiting were allowed not to understand it, and so are we.

Martha and Mary greet Him with the same sentence: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” This is what the grief of believers sounds like, and Jesus never once rebukes it. To Martha, whose theology of the resurrection “at the last day” is correct, He doesn’t correct her doctrine; He simply moves the emphasis from a distant “then” to the “now” standing in front of her: “I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this?” Hope is not a calendar of end-time events; it is a Person standing beside you. And then the shortest verse in the Bible: “Jesus wept.” The Greeks taught that you could recognize a god by his imperturbability; the Gospel shows God weeping in a cemetery. And weeping while knowing that in five minutes Lazarus would walk out. The hope of the resurrection doesn’t take away the right to grieve; it takes the hopelessness out of grief.

At the tomb Martha still protests: “By now he stinks… It has already been four days.” In the thinking of the time, the fourth day was the line of final certainty that everything was over. For God that line doesn’t exist. For the first time in this Gospel, Jesus prays aloud, addressing God as “Father,” and then calls out: “Lazarus, come out!” The dead man comes out, still wrapped in strips of linen, and then comes the final command, addressed to the people: “Unwrap him and let him go.” The miracle belongs to God; the unwrapping He left to the community. People awakened by Jesus come out of their graves still wrapped in the grave clothes of the past. A church that can only remember what someone used to smell like leaves the raised still bound.

Our section names three fears: the boat is sinking, the bread runs out, the tomb is sealed. We have already seen the storm and the hunger. Today the Gospel leads us up to the third, final wall, beyond which, humanly speaking, there is nothing. The story takes place in Bethany, a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, a brisk fifteen-minute walk from Jerusalem. The name itself says a lot: Bethany most likely means “house of the poor.” In this “house of the poor,” Jesus had a home in the warmest sense of the word: a family of friends, Martha, Mary and Lazarus, whom He visited, with whom He ate and rested. And it is from there that the news comes that everyone who loves someone dreads.

sections.heading: The One You Love Is Sick
paragraphs: The sisters’ message is a model of prayer in time of need: “Lord, the one You love is sick.” No request, no instructions, no “come at once.” The sisters don’t tell Jesus what to do; they tell Him what is happening and leave the rest to His love. That makes what follows hit all the harder: Jesus “stayed where He was for two days.” Two days of silence for a household waiting to be rescued. For centuries a charge has hung over this delay: He let His friend die so the miracle would be bigger. So it’s worth doing the arithmetic hidden in the text. Bethany lay a day’s journey from where Jesus was staying; when He arrived, Lazarus “had already spent four days in the tomb.” The messenger walked one day, Jesus waited two and walked one: four in all. That means Lazarus died at about the time the messenger was only just reaching Jesus. No immediate departure would have found him alive. The delay didn’t kill Lazarus; it only changed what Jesus would find when He arrived: fresh mourning instead of a death agony. And to the question of why He waited at all, He answers Himself: “For your sake… so that you may believe.” There are things God does in a rhythm that makes no sense to those who are waiting, and this story honestly shows that those who wait are allowed not to understand. They will understand later. Or never, and they will still be loved.

What’s more, He is going to Judea, where people had just tried to stone Him. The disciples protest, and Thomas closes the discussion with a sentence that is at once heroic and without illusions: “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.” In everyone’s eyes, this trip to Bethany was a march toward death. And in fact it was: it is the raising of Lazarus that will make the cup overflow and set in motion the decision to kill Jesus. He goes to wake His friend, knowing He will pay for it with a grave of His own.

sections.heading: If You Had Been Here
paragraphs: Martha goes out to meet Him; Mary stays at home. Both, each in her own time, will say the identical sentence: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” This is what the grief of believers sounds like: not blasphemy, not unbelief, just a painful “if only” addressed to a God who could have prevented it and didn’t. Jesus accepts that sentence twice and never once rebukes it. And the conversation with Martha becomes one of the most important dialogues in the Gospel. Martha’s theology is entirely correct: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” She confesses exactly what she was taught in the best school of thinking about the future. And Jesus doesn’t correct her confession. He simply moves the emphasis from a distant “then” to the “now” standing in front of her: “I am the resurrection and the life.” Not: there will be a resurrection. I am it. The whole series of “I am” sayings in this Gospel, from the bread of life to the gate and the shepherd, reaches its peak here, and not in a lecture hall but by the side of the road, in front of a weeping woman. Then comes the question that leaps from statements about the future to a Person: “Do you believe this?” Not “Do you affirm this thesis?” but: Do you trust Me, here, over your brother’s fresh grave? Christian hope is not a calendar of end-time events. It is a Person who stands beside you when the calendar has stopped promising anything.

sections.heading: Jesus Wept
paragraphs: Then Mary comes with the same “if You had been here,” and behind her the weeping mourners. And something happens that the Greek text describes in stronger words than translations convey. Jesus “was deeply moved in spirit”: the verb John uses denotes violent agitation with a note of anger; in classical Greek it could even describe the snorting of a horse. At His friend’s grave Jesus is not melancholy. He is shaken and angry, and that anger is aimed not at people but at death itself: the intruder that ravages God’s world and the homes of His friends. And right after that comes the shortest verse in the Bible: “Jesus wept.” To a Greek reader, this sentence was a greater scandal than the raising of the dead. The philosophers taught that the essence of divinity is apatheia, imperturbability: a god who could be moved by anything would be subject to something outside himself. Yet the Gospel shows God standing in a cemetery, weeping. And notice the strangest thing of all: He weeps knowing that in five minutes Lazarus will walk out of the tomb. That knowledge doesn’t cancel the tears. This is the answer for everyone who has ever been told that “real faith doesn’t cry, because we’ll see each other in heaven.” Jesus knew the ending better than anyone, and He wept with those who wept. The hope of the resurrection doesn’t take away the right to grieve; it only takes the hopelessness out of grief.

sections.heading: Take Away the Stone
paragraphs: Lazarus’s tomb looked like the tombs of better-off families of the time: a natural or rock-cut chamber with shelves for the bodies, closed with a heavy stone. In front of this sealed cave the final test plays out. Jesus orders the stone to be rolled away, and Martha, the same Martha who has just confessed her faith, protests: “Lord, by now he stinks… It has already been four days.” In the thinking of the time, the fourth day was the final line: it was believed that for three days there could still be some hope, but by the fourth day there was no longer any doubt that it was all over. Martha is protecting Jesus from embarrassment and herself from one last disappointment. Her “by now he stinks” is the voice of every one of us over matters that died so long ago that it no longer seems decent to pray about them. Jesus answers with a question: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” And then He does something He has never done before in this Gospel: He prays aloud, addressing God directly as “Father.” For ten chapters the Father has been spoken of in the third person; the first prayer spoken aloud to Him comes in a cemetery, beside an open grave, before witnesses, “so they may believe that You sent Me.” And finally, three words toward the dark opening: “Lazarus, come out!”

sections.heading: Unwrap Him
paragraphs: “The man who had been dead came out.” The evangelist writes that sentence as calmly as if he were describing someone stepping out of the house, and he leaves us a detail: Lazarus comes out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen and his face wrapped in a cloth. Alive, but still wrapped in death. And then Jesus gives the last command of this story, addressed not to Lazarus but to the onlookers: “Unwrap him and let him go.” The miracle belonged to God; the unwrapping He left to people. That sentence should hang over the door of every church. People come out of graves we had already buried them in: out of addiction, out of unbelief, out of old failures, out of our own judgment. And very often they come out still wrapped: smelling of the past, awkward, bound up in what used to be. The community’s role is not to check whether they are really alive. It is to unwrap them: patiently removing from a person what they were buried in, until they can walk. A church that can only remember what someone used to smell like leaves the raised still in their grave clothes.

It’s also worth seeing what this story set in motion. John goes on to say that many of the mourners believed, while the council of priests met and decided to kill Jesus. And not only Him: “So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well, for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus.” That decision says something important about the nature of testimony. Lazarus dead bothered no one; Lazarus alive became unbearable, even though the Gospel doesn’t quote a single word he said. He didn’t preach sermons. He simply lived, ate dinners and could be seen, and that was enough for people to believe. The hardest argument for Christianity to refute has never been rhetoric. It has been people who plainly came out of the grave.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If today you are standing beside something that has died, this story tells you three things. First: God’s silence is not His absence. Two days of silence didn’t mean Jesus had stopped loving the household in Bethany; there are rhythms in God’s work that you won’t understand while they are happening, and you are allowed to say out loud that you don’t understand them, as Martha and Mary did. Second: you are allowed to weep. The One who knows the ending of every story stood in a cemetery and wept; a faith that forbids tears is not the faith of Jesus. Third: for God the fourth day doesn’t exist. The line past which it “no longer seems decent” to hope is the limit of our imagination, not of His power. And the question Jesus asked Martha stands today before each of us, in the singular: I am the resurrection and the life. Do you believe this?
